title: The fire that didn't burn
hook: a messenger gives the most powerful king in the world good advice, and the king answers by setting the messenger's tail on fire
carry: sita's prayer: holding someone up from afar

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fight went on, and the rakshasas' doubting ropes undid a god's weapon. Your line: shraddha: trust given whole, not halfway.

Hanuman stands tied up before Ravana's throne, and the first thing Valmiki tells us is that Hanuman is impressed. Ravana is magnificent: radiant, crowned, mighty, surrounded by ministers. Hanuman thinks that if this king weren't so unrighteous, he could be the guardian of heaven itself. A minister asks who sent him, and Hanuman answers. Not with threats. With counsel.
screen: `HANUMAN IS IMPRESSED.` → `IF ONLY HE WERE RIGHTEOUS.` → `NOT THREATS, COUNSEL.`

segments.voice: I am Sugriva's envoy, he says, and Rama's messenger. Then he speaks to Ravana as to a king who could still choose well. You know dharma. You've gained great power through austerities. Don't throw it away for another man's wife. Give Sita back to Rama, and you can still live. Ravana's answer is rage: kill him. Then his younger brother Vibhishana speaks up. It is against dharma to kill a messenger. Punish him some other way. Ravana gives in, grudgingly. A monkey's tail is precious to him, he says. Set it on fire. So they wrap Hanuman's tail in old cloth, soak it in oil, light it, and parade him through the streets with drums. The rakshasi guards run to tell Sita. And Sita, in the grove, turns to the fire god, Agni. If I have served my husband faithfully, she prays, if I have any merit at all, be cool to Hanuman. The fire, burning brightly on his tail, does not burn him. Hanuman is astonished, and guesses it's Sita's doing, or Rama's power, or his father the wind's friendship with fire. Look at Sita here. She can't reach Hanuman. She can't fight for him. She can only pray from where she sits, and in the story, that holds him up. This is one of the quiet practices of Hindu life: praying for someone you can't reach, often with a small lamp lit at home for someone far away or in a hospital.
screen: `RETURN SITA AND BE SAVED.` · `AN ENVOY MAY NOT BE KILLED.` · `SITA PRAYS TO AGNI FROM AFAR.` · then, large: `THE FIRE DOES NOT BURN HIM.`

segments.voice: If you pray, light a small lamp or candle, or simply fold your hands, and name someone going through a fire right now: an illness, a hard week, a trial. Sita couldn't go to Hanuman; she prayed from where she was. Offer them to God in your own way. If you don't pray, send them coolness and steadiness with each breath out, and then send them a real message if you can.
The burning. Ravana rejects Hanuman's counsel, Vibhishana saves the envoy's life, and Hanuman's tail is set alight, but Sita asks the fire to be cool, and it is.
Your line: sita's prayer: holding someone up from afar. Tomorrow, the fire spreads across Lanka. Rest well.

screen: `DAY 628 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: ANGER, SHED LIKE A SKIN.`

howItsDone: The burning of Hanuman's tail and Sita's prayer to Agni are familiar scenes in Ramayana retellings; many Hindu families light a diya at home and pray for someone ill or far away, and Vibhishana's rule that an envoy must not be killed is cited by some teachers as dharma in war.

chat.meaning: Sita couldn't reach Hanuman, so she prayed to Agni from the grove, and the fire was cool to him. Hindus pray for loved ones from afar, often with a lamp.

tie.story: When Ravana set Hanuman's tail on fire, Sita, far off in the grove, prayed to Agni, and the fire did not burn him.
